Everybody warned me that I would be bored. I had lived in Oslo for nineteen years, and when I told people I was moving to a town two hours away, they looked at me as if I had lost my mind. They said I would miss the amenities. The truth is the opposite. This town has a hospital, two supermarkets, a cinema and a very good library. It has everything except the crowds. It is nowhere near as busy as Oslo, and it is considerably cheaper. My apartment in the city cost more than this whole house. Is it far quieter? Yes. It is far quieter than anywhere I had lived before, and that is exactly why I came. There is a trade-off, of course. There are fewer concerts, and the airport is a long drive. But the quiet more than makes up for it. Nobody here is in a hurry, and after nineteen years of hurrying, that is worth a great deal.

Everyone assumes I miss it. I grew up in a town of about thirty thousand people, and I could not wait to leave. When you grow up somewhere that small, everybody knows everything about you before you have decided it yourself. I wanted to be one face among millions, and that is exactly what the city gave me. People talk about the quiet as if it were a gift. Honestly, I think it is overrated. My town was not laid-back, it was slow, and there was nothing at all to do after eight in the evening. Does the city cost me something? Of course it does. I live in a cramped apartment I can barely afford, and I put up with a commute that eats an hour of every day. That is the trade-off, and I would make it again tomorrow.
